$comment: Cost-model inputs for deriving every real-time guardrail from the INR ceilings in config/environments/*.env. Per-SKU USD rates are NOT duplicated here -- src/tripplanner/validation/harness/pricing.py stays the single source for those. This file owns what pricing.py does not know: the USD->INR conversion, Google's account-wide free monthly allowances, how those pooled allowances split between environments, and the headroom used to size GCP quotas. Consumed by scripts/derive_limits.py and asserted by tests/test_limits_derivation.py.

fx.$comment: ALL ceilings and every persisted ledger amount are INR. USD appears only in provider pricing catalogs and is converted exactly once, at ledger ingestion, via cost_model.usd_to_inr(). Never compare a USD figure to an INR ceiling.

freePoolsPerMonth.$comment: Google Maps Platform free monthly allowances, pooled across EVERY project on the billing account rather than granted per project -- the three environments share one pool, so freePoolShare below must sum to <= 1.0.

freePoolShare.$comment: Share of each pooled allowance reserved per environment. Must sum to <= 1.0. Local takes the largest share because owner testing is the dominant consumer.

quotaSizing.$comment: GCP quota preferences are the real-time hard net beneath the INR ceiling. A daily quota is sized so one SKU alone cannot consume more than googleShareOfDailyCeiling of the daily INR ceiling, times dailyHeadroom. Per-MINUTE quotas are deliberately NOT cost-derived -- they exist to keep places_cache._pace() from tripping the provider circuit breaker, so they come from burstPerMinuteFloor instead.

anomaly.$comment: A trip is flagged when its INR cost exceeds BOTH ratioToMedian x the rolling median for its interaction kind AND absoluteFloorInr. The floor stops a quiet day with a tiny median from flagging every ordinary trip.

reservation.$comment: Reserve-then-reconcile. A turn reserves a pessimistic INR estimate at admission and reconciles to actual at completion, so concurrent turns cannot all pass a check each of them sees as unspent. Percentiles are computed over recent trips of the same interaction kind; seeds apply until minSamples trips exist.

cosmosSizing.$comment: Cosmos DB sizing, derived from COST_CEILING_INR_HOURLY (the burst-shaped spend ceiling) and CHAT_MAX_CONCURRENT_GLOBAL (the concurrency abuse control) rather than hand-set. Provisioned RU/s is a RATE, so it can only be derived from a rate: the daily ceiling divided by 86400 describes a smoothness real traffic never has. The chain is: hourly INR ceiling -> trips affordable in that hour -> the worst case where all of them are in flight at once (capped by the concurrency control) -> RU each trip costs -> RU/s. Consumed by scripts/derive_limits.py, asserted by tests/test_limits_derivation.py.
cosmosSizing.$ruComment: Azure's published point-operation costs: a 1 KB point read is 1 RU and a 1 KB point write about 5 RU with default (index-everything) policy, scaling with document size. These are a planning catalog exactly like GOOGLE_PLACES_USD_PER_REQUEST, not measured values -- storage_cosmos.py now captures the real x-ms-request-charge per operation, so these get replaced by observed RU once enough production traffic has accumulated.
cosmosSizing.$p95Comment: Matches reservation.seedUnknownInr.new_trip -- the same worst-case INR a new trip reserves when the ledger has no percentile history. Dividing the hourly ceiling by this is what makes 'how many trips may be in flight' a derived number.
cosmosSizing.$tripBuildComment: The chat latency SLO's p95 ceiling (azureInfraHealthAlerts chat-latency-burn alerts above 120s), so a trip build is assumed to spread its Cosmos work across at most this long. A shorter real build concentrates the same RU into less time, which is what burstFactor below covers.
cosmosSizing.$burstFactorComment: A trip build is not a smooth stream of Cosmos operations. places_cache.prefetch fans one request across places_cache._MAX_WORKERS (8) worker threads, so instantaneous RU demand runs about eight times the build-window average. Sizing RU/s on the average is what let a 400 RU/s database return 429s while its mean utilisation looked modest.
cosmosSizing.$minimumComment: 400 RU/s is Azure's floor for a shared-throughput database; the derivation may raise it but never proposes a value Cosmos would reject.
cosmosSizing.$freeTierComment: enableFreeTier on the account discounts the first 1000 RU/s ACCOUNT-WIDE, not per database -- the same pooled-allowance shape as Google's free monthly quotas, so the three environments split it through freePoolShare above. Three databases at the 400 RU/s floor already provision 1200 and bill for the overflow.

tripOpProfile.$comment: Cosmos operations one new_trip build issues, per container, with the document size used to price them. Document sizes for 'trips' are measured from corpus/trips (median 6.4 KB, p95 15.4 KB -- p95 is used, since sizing on the median is what under-provisions). The remaining rows are the call sites in each module: places_cache and tool_cache read-then-write once per resolved place or tool call for a ~5-day, ~20-place trip; provider_usage writes once per outbound provider call; trip_costs is the ledger's reserve/settle read-and-conditional-write pair per turn.

throttleAlert.$comment: The Cosmos 429 alert threshold, derived instead of the flat 20 it used to carry. A 429 is not by itself an incident -- the SDK retries it transparently -- so the threshold is the number of throttles a legitimately paced peak burst may produce across the alert window before the provisioned RU/s is genuinely wrong. Below that it is noise; above it, the derivation that produced ruPerSecond is not holding.
